unit.title: The paddock: who does what
unit.summary: Team roles, radio, teammates, the driver pipeline and the media world.

lessons.title: Who runs a team
lessons.objective: Explain what the principal, engineer and strategist each do.

payload.prompt: Match each team role to what they do.

pairs.definition: The boss who runs the team, its budget and the public face to sponsors and media.
The driver's main voice on radio: sets up the car and calls strategy decisions.
Where strategists sit trackside, reading data and making live race calls.

distractorDefinitions: The driver who leads the team in points.
The team's safety officer during pit stops.

explanation.summary: A team is three layers: the boss (principal), the driver's engineer (on radio), and the strategists (trackside data). Each has a clear job.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three jobs: the principal runs it, the engineer coaches the driver, the pit wall reads the race.

payload.prompt: What is the team principal's main job?

options.text: Running the team, the budget, and the team's image with sponsors and media.
options.explanation: Right. The principal is the boss and the public face.

options.text: Deciding pit stops and strategy calls during the race.
options.explanation: That is the pit wall and the engineer. The principal runs the team, not the race.

options.text: Driving the second car if the main driver is injured.
options.explanation: That is the reserve driver's job, not the principal's.

options.text: Tuning the car set-up before qualifying.
options.explanation: The engineer tunes the car. The principal runs the team.

explanation.correct: Right. The principal is the boss and the public face of the team to sponsors, media and the FIA.
explanation.incorrect: The team principal runs the team and its budget; they do not make race decisions or drive. That is the engineer and reserve driver.
explanation.sayThisLine: The principal runs the team; the engineer runs the race.

payload.prompt: Why is the race engineer the driver's main voice on the radio?

options.text: They know the car set-up, read data, and coach the driver through decisions.
options.explanation: Right. The engineer is the driver's single trusted source of information.

options.text: They sit with the pit wall and make all strategy calls alone.
options.explanation: The engineer relays strategy from the pit wall; they do not make calls alone.

options.text: They are the driver's teammate and help with set-up.
options.explanation: The engineer is not a driver. They are the technical coach and radio voice.

options.text: They report to the team principal between pit stops.
options.explanation: The engineer talks to the driver, not just the principal.

explanation.correct: Right. The race engineer knows the car inside out, watches the data and is the one trusted voice coaching the driver.
explanation.incorrect: The race engineer is the driver's primary coach and information source, relaying set-up changes, strategy and race situation.
explanation.sayThisLine: The engineer is the driver's coach and the pit wall's messenger.

payload.prompt: What do strategists on the pit wall do?

options.text: Read live data, watch the race, and make strategy calls: when to pit, when to save, what to do under yellows.
options.explanation: Right. The pit wall is the strategy brain, reading the race second by second.

options.text: Build and repair the car in the garage.
options.explanation: That is the mechanics' job. The pit wall is on the strategy side.

options.text: Drive the pace car if a safety car is needed.
options.explanation: The race director and FIA run safety cars; the pit wall is for strategy.

options.text: Broadcast the race on television.
options.explanation: Broadcasters work for the media; the pit wall is a team function.

explanation.correct: Right. The pit wall watches the race, reads data and tire wear, and calls the shots: pit, stay out, how to manage the gap.
explanation.incorrect: The pit wall is the race control centre for one team: data, strategy and live decision-making.
explanation.sayThisLine: The pit wall reads the race and calls strategy in real time.

payload.prompt: Match each term to what it means in the team.

pairs.definition: The driver's closest adviser: knows the car, coaches on strategy and is the single radio voice.
The trackside team who watch data, weather and other cars to guide strategy.
The team boss: runs the business, sets budgets and speaks to sponsors and media.

distractorDefinitions: The chief mechanic who oversees all pit-stop crews.
The FIA official who monitors team radio for rule breaks.

explanation.summary: Three leaders: the principal runs the team as a business; the engineer coaches the driver; the pit wall guides strategy.
explanation.sayThisLine: Principal = boss. Engineer = coach. Pit wall = strategist.

lessons.title: Reading team radio
lessons.objective: Decode common radio messages and what is really being said.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: Box box, this lap, tyres and fuel.

payload.question: What is the engineer telling the driver?

options.text: Come into the pits this lap for a tyre stop and refuelling.
options.explanation: Exactly. Box box is the pit call. But F1 has no refuelling since 2010; stops are tyres only.

options.text: The driver should stay in the pits longer than usual.
options.explanation: Box box is the call to pit, not an instruction to stay longer.

options.text: There is a problem with the brakes and the driver should box.
options.explanation: A pit call says why (fuel, tyres). If there is damage, the engineer will say so.

payload.translation: Box box means the driver should pit this lap for a tyre stop. F1 has no refuelling since 2010.

followUps.line: Why would they say 'tyres and fuel'?
followUps.why: Habit from the old days when stops included refuelling. Fans still hear it from radio archives.

followUps.line: So every pit stop is only for tyres?
followUps.why: Yes. The two-compound rule forces at least one stop, and it is always for tyres.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Box box is not an emergency. It is a normal pit call. Real emergencies use different language.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: He is lifting and coasting, trying to save fuel.

payload.question: What does lifting and coasting mean?

options.text: The driver lifts off the throttle early and coasts before braking, to save fuel or tyres.
options.explanation: Right. It costs lap time but saves fuel, battery or rubber.

options.text: The driver is taking it easy this lap.
options.explanation: It is a strategy move, not laziness. It costs time on that lap.

options.text: The car is out of fuel and rolling downhill.
options.explanation: Lifting and coasting is planned, not an emergency.

payload.translation: Lifting and coasting means the driver throttles off early before braking, trading lap time now for fuel, tyre or energy savings later.

followUps.line: Does the pit wall tell him when to lift and coast?
followUps.why: Yes, the engineer calls it based on fuel or energy math and track position.

followUps.line: Why save fuel if he can go flat out?
followUps.why: Because the race is long. If you run out near the end, you lose more time than lifting now.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Lifting and coasting is not weakness. It is a tactical choice by the strategist.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: You should hear what they say on the radio. It is hilarious and sometimes angry.

payload.question: Why do people love team radio?

options.text: It is raw emotion and real strategy talk: frustration, funny moments, and actual racing decisions unscripted.
options.explanation: Right. Team radio is real-time drama and a window into the race.

options.text: It is just the engineer giving pit calls.
options.explanation: It is more than pit calls. It is emotion, jokes, damage reports, complaints, praise.

options.text: It is boring technical talk that fans would not understand.
options.explanation: Some is technical, but fans love the raw drama and humour of real drivers.

payload.translation: Team radio is the unscripted chatter between the driver and engineer during the race: pit calls, strategy, emotion and humour.

followUps.line: Do they edit the radio for TV?
followUps.why: Yes. F1 broadcasts only radio that is interesting or relevant to the race. Beeping censors profanity.

followUps.line: Can a driver get in trouble for what they say on the radio?
followUps.why: Sometimes. The FIA can investigate unsportsmanlike or insulting language, but plain frustration is fine.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Team radio is a real thing to listen to; it helps you follow the race and feel the human side.

payload.prompt: What does the engineer say on the radio to tell the driver to pit?

options.text: Box box, this lap.
options.explanation: Right. Box box is the call to pit; the driver comes in next time around.

options.text: Stay out.
options.explanation: Stay out means do not pit yet; keep going.

options.text: Go faster.
options.explanation: That is not a pit call; it is a pace call.

options.text: Box box, not this lap.
options.explanation: That would be confusing and not used. Box box means this lap.

explanation.correct: Right. Box box this lap is the pit command. The driver pits on the next lap they are told.
explanation.incorrect: Box box is the pit call that tells the driver to come into the pits this lap.
explanation.sayThisLine: Box box means pit this lap.

lessons.title: Teammates and team orders
lessons.objective: Explain why the teammate is the true benchmark and when orders are used.

payload.prompt: Why is your teammate the fairest comparison of a driver's speed?

options.text: Because both have the same car; it is the only direct test of driver skill with equal gear.
options.explanation: Right. Different rivals have different cars and engines. Same teammate, same car.

options.text: Because the teammate is always slower and easier to beat.
options.explanation: Not always. Some drivers are beaten by their teammates; that is a hard truth.

options.text: Because rivals get more support from their team.
options.explanation: A good team backs both drivers equally; favouritism happens but it is not supposed to.

options.text: Because the leader of the championship gets the best car.
options.explanation: F1 rules say both cars are identical. In practice, it is mostly true.

explanation.correct: Right. The teammate has the same car, tyres, engine, pit crew and resources. It is the purest driver comparison.
explanation.incorrect: The teammate benchmark is the fairest because both drivers have identical cars and equipment.
explanation.sayThisLine: Your teammate drives the same car. If you lose to him, you know why.

payload.prompt: When would a team use team orders?

options.text: When winning the constructors' title is more important than two drivers fighting, or to help one driver's championship.
options.explanation: Right. The team prioritises constructors' points or one driver's title fight.

options.text: Every lap, because the team boss says so.
options.explanation: No. Teams let drivers race most of the time. Orders are rare and strategic.

options.text: To swap positions at the start so the car ahead has fresher tyres.
options.explanation: That is race strategy, not team orders. Orders are told by radio during the race.

options.text: Never, because F1 rules forbid it completely.
options.explanation: F1 allows orders for team benefit. It is tactical but sometimes controversial.

explanation.correct: Right. Team orders are used in late-race moments when the constructors' title or one driver's championship is at stake.
explanation.incorrect: Team orders are a tactical tool: the team makes one driver yield to help the other or the team's points total.
explanation.sayThisLine: Team orders mean one driver helps the other for the team's benefit.

payload.prompt: Why are team orders controversial with fans?

options.text: Because fans want to see drivers race freely; orders feel artificial and spoil the drama.
options.explanation: Right. Fans argue that orders take away racing and turn a sport into a team business.

options.text: Because orders are illegal in F1.
options.explanation: Orders are not illegal. They are allowed for team strategy.

options.text: Because they always cost the team points.
options.explanation: Orders are used to gain points, not lose them.

options.text: Because the driver who yields always quits F1.
options.explanation: Drivers move on; it is frustrating but not career-ending.

explanation.correct: Right. Many fans dislike orders because racing is the sport; a manufactured swap feels like the business side has won.
explanation.incorrect: Orders are controversial because fans value driver-versus-driver racing over team strategy.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fans want racing, not team business. Orders spoil the show.

payload.prompt: Should the team order one driver to yield?

situation.narrative: Late in the championship: your driver is second in points, 8 points behind. On lap 30 of 58, he is trailing his teammate by 2 seconds in the race, both in the points. A pit stop could swap them.

facts.label: Driver A (leader)
facts.value: Your top driver, 8 points ahead in the championship

facts.label: Driver B (trailing)
facts.value: On pace, could catch with the right pit call

facts.label: Constructors' title
facts.value: Tight; need both drivers ahead of rivals

facts.label: Pit window
facts.value: Opens in 3 laps; order now would guarantee a swap

options.label: Tell Driver B to yield to Driver A in the pit stop.
options.consequence: Driver A gets clear track and can build a gap. Constructors' points are locked in and the championship leader is protected.
considerations: The order is fair: you are not making Driver B go slower, just a pit swap.
Driver B might be frustrated, but team strategy is part of F1.
If you do not order and Driver B passes Driver A, you lose the head-to-head in points.

options.label: Let both drivers race freely; the faster one will win the pit window.
options.consequence: The drivers race and the pit wall calls the best strategy. If Driver B is faster, he earns his position. You see real pace.
considerations: This is what fans want: true racing, not team choreography.
If Driver B is quicker over the stint, he deserves to pass.
Risk: if Driver B passes and the rival team capitalizes, you lose constructors' points.

options.label: Tell Driver B to pit one lap earlier, splitting the strategies.
options.consequence: You avoid a direct order but split the pit stops. Driver B gets out ahead on fresh tyres, but the undercut might fail.
considerations: Avoids a direct order but it is still team strategy.
Offset strategies are common; fans accept this as racing.
The undercut depends on lap time; Driver B's pace will decide.

payload.expertNote: Elite teams manage this by letting the faster driver lead, then pitting strategically. Direct orders are a last resort when the title is on the line. Top teams minimize orders because they create tension.
payload.sayThisLine: Good teams let drivers race and use pit strategy to manage the outcome.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: He got out-qualified by his teammate again. Same car, so he is just slower.

payload.question: Is that the full story?

options.text: It could mean he is slower over one lap, but his race pace might be better. One qualifying does not make him slow.
options.explanation: Right. Qualifying pace and race pace are different. One result is not the whole story.

options.text: Yes, if his teammate is faster in qualifying, he is slower overall.
options.explanation: Not necessarily. Quali and race pace differ. Ask about his Sunday pace too.

options.text: He should just try harder.
options.explanation: Oversimplifies it. Quali and race pace are separate skills; the teammate battle has many laps.

payload.translation: One qualifying result does not define a driver. Some are quick for one lap but slower on race pace, or vice versa. Ask about both.

followUps.why: It matters for the grid, but grid position is not the race. Look at the full weekend and the season.

followUps.line: What is the teammate battle, then?
followUps.why: Comparing both drivers across an entire season: qualis, races, all conditions. One qualifying is a data point, not a verdict.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Do not judge a driver on one result. Ask about his race pace, his consistency and his season total.

lessons.title: The driver pipeline
lessons.objective: Explain F3, F2, super licences, junior programmes and reserves.

payload.prompt: Match each step in a driver's path to F1.

pairs.definition: F3 and F2: junior categories that are the ladder to F1, where drivers prove themselves.
The FIA licence needed to race in F1, earned by accumulating points in lower series.
Team-run academies (Red Bull, Ferrari, Mercedes) that groom and fund young drivers.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty given to drivers who break too many rules.
A special insurance policy for rookie drivers.

explanation.summary: The path is: junior series (F3, F2) → earn a super licence → join a junior programme or fight for a seat → F1.
explanation.sayThisLine: Feeder series earn points for a super licence; junior programmes speed up the journey.

options.text: The FIA licence required to race in Formula 1, earned by scoring points in F2, F3 and other junior series.
options.explanation: Right. You can not race F1 without one.

options.text: A licence you get for free once you turn 18.
options.explanation: No. You earn it by performing in junior series and accumulating super licence points.

options.text: A penalty that stops you from racing in F1.
options.explanation: A super licence is not a penalty; it is the credential to race in F1.

options.text: A certificate of driving ability for road cars.
options.explanation: A super licence is F1-specific. Road cars do not need one.

explanation.correct: Right. A super licence is the FIA document that says you are qualified to race in F1, earned through junior series results.
explanation.incorrect: A super licence is earned, not given. Drivers accumulate points in F2, F3 and lower categories to qualify.
explanation.sayThisLine: You earn a super licence in junior series; F1 requires one.

payload.prompt: What does a junior programme do?

options.text: A team academy funds, trains and grooms young drivers to reach F1; Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes run them.
options.explanation: Right. Junior programmes are talent pipelines that reduce risk for teams.

options.text: A school that teaches teenagers to drive race cars.
options.explanation: Programmes do include training, but they are part of a professional pathway, not education.

options.text: A punishment for young drivers who break F1 rules.
options.explanation: A junior programme is a promotion, not a penalty.

options.text: A lottery that picks random drivers for F1 seats.
options.explanation: Junior programmes are selective. Drivers have to earn their spot.

explanation.correct: Right. A junior programme is a team's way of developing drivers early, nurturing them through feeder series and into F1.
explanation.incorrect: Junior programmes are professional talent pipelines, not schools or lotteries.
explanation.sayThisLine: Junior programmes fund drivers on the way up. Being picked is a big deal.

payload.prompt: What does a reserve driver do?

options.text: Stands by to race if a main driver is sick or injured. Stays sharp with simulations and practice.
options.explanation: Right. The reserve is the backup and often a junior-programme driver.

options.text: Drives the second car in every race.
options.explanation: No. A reserve only drives if the main driver cannot. The second seat is a race driver.

options.text: Manages the team's spare cars and pit equipment.
options.explanation: That is a team role, not a driver role. The reserve is a racing licence.

options.text: Replaces the team principal if the boss quits.
options.explanation: A reserve is a racing driver, not a business manager.

explanation.correct: Right. The reserve driver is the team's backup racing licence, called up if a race driver cannot compete.
explanation.incorrect: A reserve driver is a backup: they train, simulate and race only if needed.
explanation.sayThisLine: The reserve races when the main driver cannot.

payload.prompt: Match each role or stage to what it is.

pairs.definition: The main feeder series where drivers prove themselves before F1, step below the world championship.
A driver funded and trained by Red Bull's academy, groomed for Red Bull or sister-team seats.
The third driver at a team, standing by in case the main race driver is unavailable.

distractorDefinitions: A driver who finished second in the championship.
A driver who quit racing to become a broadcaster.

explanation.summary: The path: feeder series (F2, F3) → maybe a junior programme → reserve role → race seat.
explanation.sayThisLine: Feeder series, then junior academy, then reserve, then racing.

lessons.title: Silly season, tifosi and the Netflix effect
lessons.objective: Explain the driver market and how fandom works.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: Silly season has started. Everyone is guessing about next year's seats.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Mid-season driver-market speculation: who will drive for which team next year. Lots of gossip and rumours.
options.explanation: Right. Silly season is the time when the paddock buzzes with seat moves.

options.text: A time when drivers make mistakes and crash.
options.explanation: Not mistakes; speculation and rumours about contracts.

options.text: It is just gossip, not real news.
options.explanation: It starts as gossip but often leads to real announcements. It is the paddock's main sport.

payload.translation: Silly season is mid-season speculation and rumours about which drivers will move to which teams for next year.

followUps.line: Why is it called silly season?
followUps.why: Because the paddock turns into a rumour mill. Things are announced, denied, then revealed as half-truths.

followUps.line: Does silly season affect the race?
followUps.why: Sometimes. A driver rumoured to be leaving plays harder. Uncertainty can help or hurt performance.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Silly season is real speculation, not just fun. Contract news moves drivers, teams and the championship.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: The tifosi flooded the track after the race. Monza always goes wild.

payload.question: Who are the tifosi?

options.text: Ferrari's famously passionate fans, especially in Italy. They create incredible atmosphere.
options.explanation: Right. The tifosi are legendary for their noise, colour and passion.

options.text: All F1 fans around the world.
options.explanation: Tifosi is specifically Ferrari's fanbase, not all fans.

options.text: Italian police who manage crowds at the track.
options.explanation: Tifosi are fans, not police. The word is Italian for supporters.

payload.translation: The tifosi are Ferrari's passionate fanbase, especially strong in Italy. They create an electric atmosphere at Monza.

followUps.line: Why do the tifosi flood the track?
followUps.why: It is a tradition of celebration and loyalty. The FIA tries to stop it for safety, but it keeps happening.

followUps.line: Is Ferrari the only team with passionate fans?
followUps.why: No, but Ferrari fans are the most organized and famous for showing up in huge numbers.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Tifosi are fans, and fandom is part of the sport. Learn the culture, do not judge it.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: F1 has so many new fans thanks to Drive to Survive. The energy is different now.

payload.question: What is Drive to Survive?

options.text: A Netflix series that dramatizes F1 life, paddock politics and driver stories. It brought millions of new fans, especially younger viewers.
options.explanation: Right. Drive to Survive opened F1 to people who never watched before.

options.text: A racing sim game on streaming.
options.explanation: It is a documentary series, not a game.

options.text: The official F1 broadcast on TV.
options.explanation: Drive to Survive is Netflix, independent from F1's broadcast deals.

payload.translation: Drive to Survive is a Netflix documentary series that dramatizes F1 team life, rivalries and driver personalities. It introduced millions to the sport.

followUps.line: Does Drive to Survive show real races?
followUps.why: It mixes race footage with behind-the-scenes drama and interviews. Not every moment is race action.

followUps.line: Do long-time F1 fans like it?
followUps.why: Mixed. Some love the new fans it brings; others find the drama exaggerated. It is a cultural moment either way.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Drive to Survive is entertainment. Real F1 is deeper than Netflix drama, but both matter now.

options.text: The hospitality and team area behind the pits where drivers, engineers and team staff live during a race weekend.
options.explanation: Right. The paddock is the backstage world of F1: where deals happen, teams strategize, and drama unfolds.

options.text: The area where fans stand to watch the race.
options.explanation: Fans are in the grandstands and general admission. The paddock is team territory only.

options.text: The pit lane where cars are repaired.
options.explanation: The pit lane is separate. The paddock is the hospitality and motorhome area.

options.text: The track where the race happens.
options.explanation: The track is the circuit. The paddock is the team area behind the pits.

explanation.correct: Right. The paddock is the team sector: motorhomes, hospitality, engineers' offices and media zones behind the pits.
explanation.incorrect: The paddock is the F1 social world: team bases, press centres and where the sport's people live during a race weekend.
explanation.sayThisLine: The paddock is backstage: where teams live and deal-making happens.

options.text: Driver loyalty, paddock drama, rivalries and the culture of teams and fans. Personality and story matter as much as speed.
options.explanation: Right. F1 is as much about people as it is about racing now.

options.text: Betting and predictions on race outcomes.
options.explanation: Betting exists, but F1 marketing does not push it. The sport is about fandom, not wagering.

options.text: The fastest driver always winning every race.
options.explanation: That is not how F1 works. Strategy, pit cycles, luck and reliability change the race.

options.text: Sponsorship logos and team budgets.
options.explanation: Sponsors matter to teams, but fans care about drivers, rivals and the story of the season.

explanation.correct: Right. F1 fandom is personal: you pick a driver or team and follow their journey, rivalry and drama.
explanation.incorrect: F1 fandom is built on stories: driver loyalty, team rivalries, paddock drama and the culture of the sport.
explanation.sayThisLine: F1 is not just racing. It is fandom, loyalty and the culture of the paddock.
